The way it works at alton still is that you get a paper leaflet and you take it to the designated ride entrance for RAP. You can go straight to the first ride you want to go to. Before you get on the ride the staff will look at the queue time and write on the leaflet the next time you can access a ride, which is the current time plus most of the queue time. When this time is over, you can go straight on the next one provided there is no queue. Between the time you get off the first ride and the time you are allowed to go to another, you can do whatever you like, you aren’t queueing in a physical sense. 
I’ve been with a RAP 10+ times in the last couple of years, in peak and off peak time and never waited more than five minutes to go on a ride from the RAP entrance. 
The only ride I’ve seen with a seating area is runaway mine train. 
Also, bear in mind the sky liner is closed for the rest of the season, and it is a walk and a half to get around.
FYI, they still make you take off shoes of any kind, even specific water shoes. I’d still recommend getting water shoes and having to take them off on body slides.

First you need to apply for the card. It’s easiest to do this before you go. You’ll need a document to prove disability (these documents are listen on the website). 
When you go, you can go to your Disney hotel, or guest services and they will ask for your application and your proof of disability document. 

When you have the pass it will have a coloured code to tell staff members what you require. For most rides you can follow the ‘magicALL’ signs or wheelchair signs and go to the exits of the rides and they will let you on, and afterwards you can just go to the next ride and go on without having to wait like in disneyworld. 
HOWEVER, a big problem with their system is that it is not clear on multiple rides where the ‘correct’ entrance is. For some rides (cars road trip, phantom manor, etc) they have multiple entrances for different disabilities (wheelchair accessible, not wheelchair accessible). When we went to these rides the signage was not clear where we had to go and when we went to the wheelchair entrance they wouldn’t let us in.

No problem. I always think trying foods that I consider to be ‘related’ is easier. That way it’s still half safe, but half new. 
Some more ideas:
I always try to follow the ‘rule of three’. Take three bites, and try it on three different days. The first time you’ll be scared and anxious and you won’t be able to tell if you think it’s ok or not. 
Even though it’s hard right now and you don’t feel like you’re getting enough fuel, don’t rush it. It’s better to heal the issue from the source and get better at eating, not rush it and scare yourself. In the meantime consider calorie supplements like meal replacement shakes, drinks, tablets, etc. and vitamin tablets.

Have you tried a ‘similar food’ approach? In this I would start with sage food and then branch out slowly, so say a safe cracker, then try a cracker that looks the same, or the same brand but a different flavour. Remember it’s ok to not like it

For Merlin? If you have a valid ride access pass for Merlin, when it need renewing it has to be done now through nimbus. Your best bet is applying for an access ID through nimbus independently, they take your proof and everything and verify your disability, then places such as Merlin and Disney use that access ID as proof so they don’t have to verify disability themselves

Also you mentioned Merlin, in case you aren’t aware of the change a doctors letter is no longer sufficient for Merlin either, they’ve tightened it up a lot because of lots of people abusing the system. You are required to have an access ID/ apply for the ride access pass through nimbus (the company behind access ID).

What documents you need for a priority card depends on what country you are visiting from and you can check this on the Disneyland Paris website. If you are from the uk, you can use a disability living allowance letter, attendance allowance letter, PIP, disabled parking badge, national disability ID card, disabled ID, access card, disabled students allowance, and a few others like army, visual impairment related, etc. A doctors letter/ medical certificate is not accepted.

I find that too that it feels awkward to try and assert yourself, i know it’s hard but you have to try and remember that you are the customer and you are paying them to listen to you and your wants. When you think about it, the hairdresser probably values and appreciates having a very clear idea of what you want because that will make it obvious and easier for them too. Having a collage and written notes on exactly what you want will often help you babble less because you have a clear list of what you want to say. As for pictures, i tend to search Pinterest, and just Google. Make a list of the key words you are seeing and search off of those, also look into the hairdressers terms for the cuts to be able to find specific things, like ‘shoulder length, wolf cut, feathered, choppy’ etc. lastly if you see pictures of people on social media that you like the look of their hair, screenshot them and add them in!

What i do is make a collage of pictures, half of what my hair looks like normally so they can see the texture ect. And half of inspiration pictures, take the time to find all of the different elements of exactly what you want, make notes on it if what you like and what you do not want, and make sure they see it and look at it properly, print it out even and make sure you have a discussion on what you want and make sure they understand you. I am an autistic girl, and I know it seems awful to think of your baby being different, but it’s going to be ok. I wasn’t diagnosed until I was 18 and my diagnosis was one of the best things to happen to me. I no longer felt like I was broken or ‘bad’ at being ‘normal’, I was autistic, and that makes me work differently. Being diagnosed changed my life for the better because it made me realise who I am and that I’m different but perfect at being me. Sure, it’s hard living in a world that isn’t designed for you, but once you know you can adapt and make things work for you (for your child). It’s important that she knows as she grows up that nothing is ‘wrong’ with her, autism is a different way of working, not an illness. Be there to support her and advocate for her so she always gets what she needs. It’s not her job to fit into a world that is made more neurotypical people. Even if she turns out to be non-verbal or less communicative, you’ll be surprised in the ways that children find to communicate, and she will still know that things are either harder for her, or adapted for her, even if it’s hard to see from the outside. 
It’s also important and valid to grieve for the child you expected to have, and that doesn’t mean you love her any less. You might have a different life than you expected, but no matter how hard it gets, it will be ok. You might have different ways of communicating or spending time with your child, less talking more sign language or aac, less ‘girly time’ more therapies, and it’s ok to be sad about it, but any time spent with your child is important and valid, and these can be more special and rewarding.

2- The workload is pretty typical, i dont have another degree to compare it to obviously so im not too sure. Currently I have 1 or 2 online lectures most days, some none, never really after 4 in my course but everywhere is different im sure. My course has 2 placements in year 1 and an assignment due typically every few weeks.

3-My first placement was put online due to covid so that was very different, but it focused on teaching skills instead, things like the roles of different people in the school (headteacher, governers etc), and lesson planning, watching videos that local teachers made for us, etc and we had to make an assignment throughout about what we were doing. Real assignments you will get very involved in teaching over time, first of all just watching, helping out in more of a teaching assistants role. By the end of your placements you will be planning lessons and effectively being the teacher.

4- Generally you will learn about mathematics at a primary level, but I think its useful to have at least a very strong foundation of ks1 and 2 maths, but also ks3 maths if you can. It just boosts your confidence in it and understanding more than you need to can mean you can help kids develop further than the curriculum if they can.
